title: God Has No Body or Shape
english: For what is free of body would also be free of shape, since the divine has neither size nor shape.
But if they think that God himself, who is over all, was shaped after the nature of the human body, let them say whether he too has feet to walk with, hands to work with, and eyes to see with.
Where, then, does he walk?
Or from what place does he go, and to what place, he who fills all things?
For he said, “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24).
And what hands does he set to work, he who creates through the living Word?
And if, like us, he has eyes set in a face, then surely he does not see what is behind him.
When he looks toward the east, is he then unaware of what people in the west are doing?
And when he turns to the west again, can he not see those in the east?
I am ashamed even to write these things, but because of the senselessness of some I have become a fool (2 Corinthians 12:11).
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76 Ad Calosyrium (CPG 5230), Greek, via the Khazarzar transcription. This section continues the argument of the previous one ('nor is he in bodily form'), hence the opening 'For'.

The Greek section ends at γέγονα ('I have become'); its predicate ἄφρων ('a fool') stands at the head of the next section. The English completes the clause here ('I have become a fool'), and the next section gives the rest of it.
ἄποσον means without quantity or size; ἀσχημάτιστον, without shape.
ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων Θεός ('God, who is over all') may echo Romans 9:5; it is not cited inline because the wording is a common title.
διὰ ζῶντος Λόγου: Cyril means the Son, hence 'the living Word' with a capital W; a possible allusion to John 1:3, not cited inline.
The east and west questions draw out the absurd result: if God had eyes in a face, he could not see behind him.

title: What the Image of God Means
english: Not willingly, but because they have forced me.
So let those who babble such things be silenced, as the ignorant people they are; let them keep quiet and not meddle with what is beyond their power, or rather, let them stop speaking against God.
For God is above all creation: he is not conceived as a body, nor in bodily forms or shapes.
He is simple, immaterial, without form, and not composite; he is not put together from parts, limbs, or members as we are.
Rather, as the Scriptures say, he is spirit (John 4:24); he looks upon all things, is present everywhere, fills all things, and is absent from nothing.
For he fills heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24).
The statement that man was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27) bears another sense and points to another meaning.
For of all the living creatures on earth he alone is rational and compassionate, with an aptitude for every virtue, and he has also been given the power to rule.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76 Ad Calosyrium (CPG 5230), Greek, via the Khazarzar transcription.

The section opens with the end of a clause begun in the previous section (γέγονα | ἄφρων, οὐχ ἑκὼν μᾶλλον, ἀλλὰ παρ' αὐτῶν ἠναγκασμένος). 'I have become a fool' is given there; this section gives the rest as 'Not willingly, but because they have forced me.' The 2 Corinthians 12:11 citation stands once, in the previous section.
ἐπιστομιζέσθωσαν (literally 'be muzzled') is rendered 'be silenced'; a possible echo of Titus 1:11, not cited inline.
ἠρεμείτωσαν picks up ἠρεμεῖν in the opening section ('those who wish to live in quiet'); rendered 'keep quiet' to keep the link.
μὴ καταλαλείτωσαν (present imperative with μή) is rendered 'let them stop speaking against God'.
πνεῦμα is kept lowercase ('he is spirit') because Cyril speaks of the divine nature, not of the Holy Spirit as a Person.
ἑτέρας ἐμφάσεις καὶ ὑπονοίας: 'another sense ... another meaning', that is, other than a bodily sense.
The Greek section ends at τὸ ἄρχειν ('to rule'); its object opens the next section, where the English resumes with 'He holds rule over all that is on the earth'.

title: The Image Is Not the Body's Shape
english: He holds rule over all that is on the earth, after the likeness and image of God (Genesis 1:26).
So it is because he is a rational living being, a lover of virtue, and a ruler over the things of the earth that he is said to have been made in the image of God.
But if they think the image refers to the shape of the body, then nothing stops them from saying that God shares the form of the brute animals as well.
For we see that they too are made of the same parts as we are: they have feet and a mouth, eyes, nostrils and a tongue, and the other members of the body.
Let your Reverence, then, put a stop to such people, or rather, rebuke those who make a habit of babbling such things.
I hear, too, that they say the mystical blessing has no power to sanctify if any of it is left over until another day.
They are mad to say this.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76 Ad Calosyrium (CPG 5230), Greek, via the Khazarzar transcription.

The section opens with the object of λαχὼν δὲ καὶ τὸ ἄρχειν at the end of the previous section; the English resumes the clause as a full sentence ('He holds rule over ...'). καθ' ὁμοιότητα καὶ εἰκόνα Θεοῦ may qualify the rule alone or the whole list (reason, compassion, virtue, rule); the next sentence shows Cyril means the whole list, and the English keeps the phrase where he puts it.
The second mention of the image (ἐν εἰκόνι Θεοῦ πεποιῆσθαι) is not cited again inline; Genesis 1:27 is cited in the previous section and Genesis 1:26 one sentence earlier.
οὐδὲν λυπεῖ is the idiom 'nothing prevents', rendered 'nothing stops them'.
ἡ σὴ θεοσέβεια is an honorific address to Bishop Calosyrius (literally 'your reverence for God'), rendered 'your Reverence'.
ἡ μυστικὴ εὐλογία ('the mystical blessing') is Cyril's term for the consecrated Eucharist; the question is whether a portion kept to a later day still sanctifies. The English keeps his word.
The section ends at 'They are mad to say this.' The Greek goes on with οὐ γὰρ ('For ... not'), the start of the next sentence, which belongs to the rest of the letter and is not translated here.
